Pd/Brønsted Acid Co-catalyzed Dehydrative Coupling of Propargylic
Alcohols with Diarylphosphine Oxides
Zhaoqiang Chen and Hui Qian*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2025, 27, 522−527

ABSTRACT: An efficient dehydrative coupling of propargylic
alcohols with diarylphosphine oxides to construct tetrasubstituted
allenylphosphoryl compounds in the presence of a Pd/Brønsted
acid co-catalyst has been developed. As a benefit from the use of a
Brønsted acid, this reaction could perform under mild conditions
with excellent yields, accommodating a wide range of functional
groups. The potential utility of this method has also been
demonstrated.
T
he ongoing advancement of phosphorus chemistry
remains a topic of enduring significance due to the
diverse applications in pharmaceutical science,
1
materials
chemistry,
2
and organic chemistry.
3
Introducing phosphorus
atoms into organic molecules could result in substantial
modifications to their chemical and physical properties,
rendering phosphination a commonly employed efficient
method for generating innovative compounds. Allenyl
phosphine oxides, specific types of P-functionalized unsatu-
rated compounds, have garnered considerable interest in
recent years due to their distinctive allenic structure and
phosphorus functionality, which embedded them with unique
reactive and biological activities.
4−7
Therefore, increasing
attention has been focusing on the advancement of novel
methodologies to acquire phosphorus-substituted allenes. The
traditional approach for their preparation mainly relies on the
Horner−Mark rearrangement reaction, which underwent an
intermediate of propargyl phosphate (Scheme 1a).
8
Although
delivering the desired allenylphosphoryl compounds, it
suffered from toxic and unstable reagents as well as a limited
substrate scope. To overcome these issues, transition-metal
(TM)-catalyzed coupling of propargylic derivatives with
readily available and stable secondary phosphine oxides has
been called in for the synthesis of such compounds (Scheme
1b).
9
The direct dehydrate C−P coupling of propargylic
alcohols is the most straightforward and efficient strategy;
however, the C−O bond is much more inert and less reactive.
Therefore, Lewis acid catalysts had been applied in such
transformations with a high temperature (Scheme 1c).
10
Inspired by previous work,
11
a catalytic amount of Brønsted
acid could facilitate the hydroxy group to form a transient
leaving group and could be further converted to construct the
C−C bond in the presence of a palladium catalyst. Here, we
reported the dehydrative C−P coupling of propargylic alcohols
with Pd/H
+
co-catalysis, affording the tetrasubstituted
allenylphosphoryl compounds under mild conditions with
broad functional group compatibility.

With the optimized conditions in hand, we next explored the
reaction scope (Scheme 2). Propargylic alcohols bearing a
wide range of aryl groups with electron-donating (1b−1e) and
electron-withdrawing (1f−1i) substituents all reacted smoothly
with diphenylphosphine oxide 2a, forming the corresponding
tetrasubstituted allenylphosphoryl products (3ba−3ia) in
decent to excellent yields. It is worth mentioning that the
steric effect seems to have no impact because substrates
containing a methyl group at the ortho, meta, and para
positions of the phenyl group all produced the intended
products (3ba−3da) in significant yields. The reaction of 2-
(naphthalen-2-yl)oct-3-yn-2-ol also performed well under the
standard conditions, giving an 88% yield of allene product 3ja.
Heteroaryl groups, such as furyl and thienyl, also furnished
target products 3ka and 3la in decent yields. The R
2
group
may also be alkyl groups (3ma−3oa). However, when a
sterically hindered tert-butyl group was employed, the allene
product 3pa could be afforded in only a 11% yield with a 79%
recovery of raw materials. Then, we set out to investigate the
R
1
group with diverse alkyl and aryl substituents: an array of
propargylic alcohols bearing different lengths of alkyl chains or
containing useful handles were all examined, affording the
allene products 3qa−3va in excellent yields. Besides, the R
1
group may also be an aryl group (1w−1A), providing the
related allene products (3wa−3Aa) and showing a better
conversion efficiency with more electron-deficient substrates.
The structure of product 3Aa was confirmed by single-crystal
X-ray diffraction analysis. In addition, there was no effect on
the reaction when we replaced R
3
with an ethyl group (1B and
1C) or propyl group (1D). Meanwhile, reactions of other
diarylphosphine oxides, including halides (F and Br) and
trifluoromethyl substituents, had also been studied, providing
allene possessing different kinds of phosphoryl groups with
good yields (3ab−3ad). Finally, we also performed the C−P
coupling reaction with H-phosphonates. Diethyl phosphite 2e
exhibited a low reactivity, and only 10% yield of product 3ae
could be supplied. When compound 2e was replaced with
cyclic H-phosphonate 2f, the corresponding products 3af and
3wf could be obtained with satisfactory results.

To gain insight into the mechanism, kinetic studies were
conducted and showed that the reaction was first-order in the
catalyst and Brønsted acid (Scheme 4). These data indicated
that both palladium catalyst and phosphoric acid were essential
for facilitating the conversion of propargylic alcohol to allene.
These findings were also consistent with the results of the
controlling experiments (entries 14 and 15 of Table 1). On the
basis of the above experimental results and previous
reports,
11,12
a possible catalytic cycle was proposed in Scheme
5,
13
in which propargylic alcohol 1 would be activated by
Brønsted acid to yield oxonium intermediate I, which would
easily undergo an anti-oxidative addition with palladium(0) to
deliver allenyl palladium intermediate II. Then, a ligand-
exchange process would happen between intermediate II and
in situ-generated tautomeric P(III). Subsequent reductive
elimination formed the desired product and regenerated the
palladium(0) species.

In summary, we have developed an efficient strategy for the
dehydrative coupling to produce the corresponding tetrasub-
stituted allenylphosphoryl products. The key to our protocol
mainly relies on the introduction of Brønsted acid to enhance
the leaving ability of the hydroxyl group, which makes the
reaction work well under mild conditions with better substrate
compatibility. Further studies are currently ongoing in our
laboratory.

Brønsted acid, this reaction could perform under mild conditions
with excellent yields, accommodating a wide range of functional
groups. The potential utility of this method has also been
demonstrated.

dehydrative coupling to produce the corresponding tetrasub-

mainly relies on the introduction of Brønsted acid to enhance
the leaving ability of the hydroxyl group, which makes the
reaction work well under mild conditions with better substrate
compatibility. Further studies are currently ongoing in our
